title: GM Expands ‘Eyes‑Off’ Autonomous Driving to Pickup Trucks and SUVs, Boosting Future Mobility
body:
General Motors announced a major extension of its “eyes‑off” autonomous‑driving suite, rolling the technology out to a broader lineup that now includes its most popular pickups and sport‑utility vehicles. The move signals GM’s accelerating push into artificial‑intelligence‑driven software as a core profit center, positioning the Detroit‑based automaker to compete not only with traditional rivals but also with tech‑heavy newcomers vying for dominance in the future of mobility.

The new rollout will see the Super Cruise hands‑free system, which already powers a limited set of Cadillac and Chevrolet models, integrated into the upcoming Chevrolet Silverado, GMC Sierra, Chevrolet Tahoe, and GMC Yukon. By extending the feature to trucks and larger SUVs, GM is targeting segments that historically generate the highest average transaction prices and profit margins. Analysts estimate that the addition of “eyes‑off” capability could lift the average selling price of these models by roughly 2‑3 percent, a modest yet meaningful boost in an industry where incremental pricing pressure is intense.

Industry insiders note that the expansion reflects GM’s broader strategy to transform from a pure‑vehicle manufacturer into a “software and services” company. Over the past two years, the company has poured billions into its Ultium battery platform, its Cruise autonomous‑driving subsidiary, and a suite of in‑vehicle connectivity tools. Executives argue that the recurring revenue streams from subscription‑based driver assistance, over‑the‑air updates, and data‑analytics services will eventually eclipse traditional hardware sales. In this context, the decision to embed Super Cruise in high‑volume models is less about immediate profit from the feature itself and more about building a massive installed base that can be monetized through future software upgrades and mobility services.

The timing also coincides with a tightening regulatory environment and shifting consumer expectations. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration has been urging automakers to adopt advanced driver‑assistance systems (ADAS) as a pathway to reducing traffic fatalities. Meanwhile, a growing segment of buyers—particularly younger, tech‑savvy consumers—are willing to pay a premium for vehicles that can handle highway driving with minimal driver input. By making hands‑free capability a standard offering on its flagship trucks and SUVs, GM hopes to capture this emerging demand and differentiate itself from competitors that still limit such technology to luxury sedans or niche models.

However, the rollout is not without challenges. Integrating high‑level autonomy into larger, heavier vehicles demands rigorous testing to ensure sensor fidelity, braking performance, and lane‑keeping precision under diverse weather and road conditions. Critics point out that previous iterations of Super Cruise required drivers to keep their eyes on the road, a limitation that may deter some users seeking a truly hands‑free experience. GM has responded by promising software updates that will enhance driver monitoring and expand the system’s operational design domain, but the company will need to demonstrate reliability at scale to avoid reputational setbacks.

Looking ahead, GM’s expansion of “eyes‑off” technology could serve as a springboard for more ambitious autonomous initiatives, such as fully driverless ride‑hailing fleets and long‑haul trucking services. The company has already signaled intentions to leverage its Cruise subsidiary for commercial deployments, and a larger fleet equipped with advanced ADAS will provide valuable data to refine the underlying AI algorithms. If GM can successfully monetize these software capabilities while maintaining safety standards, the automaker may usher in a new era where revenue is increasingly decoupled from vehicle sales and tied to ongoing digital services. The coming years will reveal whether this strategic bet pays off, but the message is clear: GM is betting heavily on software to drive its next wave of growth.
